The writer effectively engages multiple senses to make the setting feel tangible and real. They appeal to the sense of touch (the crust of dry earth crumbling in Ines's hand, the lock giving way without resistance), smell (the scent of "cold lime" and sweetish floor wax in the hallway), sight (the gray coat with the inside-out sleeve, the crescent-shaped burn mark on the oilcloth, the steep handwriting on the pear jars, the brass weight of the clock), and sound (the familiar, steady ticking of the pendulum clock). These specific sensory details ground the reader in the environment and heighten the eerie atmosphere of the final twist.
